Fix Gradle build/run configuration for Pan
commitResults.messageBody:
The build.gradle still carried the template defaults, so `./gradlew run`
and the built JAR failed with ClassNotFoundException for seedu.duke.Duke.

- Point application.mainClass at the real entry point, pan.Pan
- Rename the shadowJar output from duke.jar to pan.jar for consistency
- Move TestPan.java (a manual, non-JUnit harness) out of src/main so it
  is no longer compiled into the production build / shipped in the JAR;
  it now lives in src/test/java
- Set test.failOnNoDiscoveredTests = false so the :test task doesn't fail
  now that test sources exist but hold no JUnit tests yet

Verified: `./gradlew clean build`, `./gradlew run`, and
`java -jar build/libs/pan.jar` all work.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add find command to search tasks by keyword
Add JavaFX GUI for the PanPan chatbot
commitResults.messageBody:
Level-10 adds a windowed front end alongside the existing console one,
following the se-education JavaFX tutorial (Parts 1-4).

Build:
- Add the JavaFX 23.0.1 dependencies (base, controls, fxml, graphics)
  for all three OSes so the fat JAR runs on any of them.
- Point application.mainClass at a new pan.Launcher, which does not
  extend Application; this avoids the "JavaFX runtime components are
  missing" error when JavaFX is on the classpath rather than the
  module path.

Shared logic:
- Ui methods now return their text as Strings instead of printing it,
  so the console loop and the GUI reuse the exact same wording.
- Pan.getResponse(String) turns one input line into one reply and is
  called by both front ends; Pan.isExit() lets the GUI close the
  window after "bye". The console Pan.main path still works.

GUI:
- Main loads MainWindow.fxml and injects the Pan back end.
- MainWindow is the controller wiring the text field and Send button.
- DialogBox loads DialogBox.fxml through the fx:root construct: one
  chat bubble per message, avatar flipped for PanPan's replies.
- Avatar images added under src/main/resources/images/.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add assertions to document internal invariants
commitResults.messageBody:
PanPan had several assumptions that were only implicit in comments
or Javadoc (e.g. "already range-checked by the caller"). Use Java's
assert feature to make these assumptions explicit and checkable
during development/testing, without affecting production behaviour
(assertions are off by default unless run with -ea).

 Assertions added:
  - TaskList.get/remove: index is within bounds, per the existing
    Javadoc contract with Pan.parseTaskNumber.
  - Pan.parseTaskNumber: postcondition that the returned index is
    valid, self-checking the method's own range-check logic.
  - Deadline/Event constructors: by/start/end are never null, since
    Parser's date methods always return a value or throw.
  - TaskList.find: keyword is never null, since Parser.arguments()
    never returns null.

Deliberately did not add an assertion in Storage.parseTask for a
malformed save-file line. That failure is a real, expected case
(a corrupted or old-format file), not a programming bug, and is
already handled by catching RuntimeException in load(). An
AssertionError would not be caught there (it extends Error, not
RuntimeException), so using assert would either crash the app
(with -ea) or silently do nothing (without it, the default).

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract one handler method per command
commitResults.messageBody:
getResponse() had grown to 70 lines. Its switch also mixed levels of
abstraction: some cases were a single high-level call, while others
dropped into index arithmetic, persistence and message formatting.
That breaks two guidelines from the course's code quality chapter,
"Avoid Long Methods" and "SLAP Hard".

The low-level steps were duplicated across those cases as well:

- storage.save(tasks.asList()) appeared six times
- the add-save-confirm sequence appeared three times
- the "arguments are empty" guard appeared three times

Give each command its own private handler so the switch reads as a
table of contents, and pull the repeated steps into addTask(),
saveTasks() and requireArguments(). Handing addTask() the task it
should add also retires the tasks.get(tasks.size() - 1) idiom, which
worked only because add() happens to append.

Deadline and event dispatch straight to addTask() rather than through
a handler of their own, since such a handler would only forward.

This is behaviour preserving: every user-visible message and every
error condition is unchanged, including the deliberate difference
where "delete" with no arguments complains about the missing task
while "mark" with no arguments complains about the missing number.
Verified by replaying one scripted session against the pre-refactor
and post-refactor builds: identical transcripts and save files.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Extract one handler method per command

commitResults.messageTitle: Add update command to edit a task in place
commitResults.messageBody:
Fixing a typo, or shifting an event's end time by an hour, meant
deleting the task and adding it again. That loses its position in the
list and its done/not-done status, and makes the user retype details
that were not wrong.

Add "update TASK_NUMBER /OPTION NEW_VALUE", which changes one detail
and leaves everything else alone:

    update 3 /to 2019-10-15 1900

/desc works on any task, /by on a deadline, /from and /to on an event.

Which option maps to which field depends on the kind of task, so that
decision lives in the task classes: Task.applyUpdate() handles /desc
and rejects anything it does not know, and Deadline and Event override
it for their own dates before deferring to super. The update command
therefore never has to ask what type of task it is holding.

Parsing reuses Parser.commandWord()/arguments(), which already split a
first word from the rest -- once to take the task number off the front,
once to take the option name off its value. Parser.parseDateTime() is
reused for the new date, so a bad date gives the same yyyy-MM-dd HHmm
hint the deadline and event commands already give.

Only one option is accepted per command. The alternative, accepting
several, would either silently fold a mistyped second option into the
first one's value, or need every value validated up front to stop a
task being left half-changed. One option per command avoids both: a
rejected update throws before assigning anything, so the task and the
save file are untouched.

Cover the new parsing and the polymorphic update in ParserTest and a
new TaskTest, including that changing an event's end time leaves its
start, description and done status as they were.

Add update command to edit a task in place

commitResults.messageTitle: Make PanPan's voice consistent across all messages
commitResults.messageBody:
The chatbot's personality had drifted as features were added, so the
same bot sounded like three different products depending on which
command you typed.

Four rules now hold across all 30 user-facing messages:

- every message is a different sentence
- PanPan always refers to itself in the third person
- exactly half the messages (15 of 30) carry a kaomoji
- every message starts with a leading space

Three defects blocked those rules and are fixed here:

- Ui.showLoadingError() was dead code holding a duplicate of the
  message Storage.load() already prints inline, so it is deleted.
  Nothing called it; runtime behaviour is unchanged.
- Parser threw the identical "OOPS!!! An event needs both /from and
  /to" for two different mistakes. It now says which half is missing,
  so the message is useful as well as unique.
- Three messages were still the original template's wording with no
  "PanPan" in them: the find header, the task count after a delete,
  and the "OOPS!!!" above.

Beyond those, the four missing-argument errors in Pan all opened with
the same "Ehhh? PanPan is confused..." phrase and now each have their
own; one kaomoji that appeared four times is down to two; the greeting
gained the leading space every other message already had; and the
unmark confirmation lost a stray "!:".

Wording only -- no logic changes, and no test asserts on message text,
so the suite is untouched.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Restyle the chat window and crop avatars to circles
commitResults.messageBody:
The GUI was stock JavaFX: grey Modena chrome, square 100x100 avatars
and no stylesheet at all. At the window's 400px width each avatar ate
a quarter of every row, which is the display space the brief asks us
not to waste on background.

Add view/styles.css, a "Bamboo Blush" theme of a cream page, white
bubbles for PanPan and pink ones for the user. The pink is taken from
the blush both avatars already wear, so the artwork and the window
agree. Colours and padding live in the stylesheet rather than the
FXML, so the look can change without touching the layout.

Space reclaimed:

- avatars drop from 100px to 40px, giving ~60px per row back to text
- the ScrollPane's vbarPolicy moves from ALWAYS to AS_NEEDED, which
  was costing ~10px of width even in an empty window
- the ScrollPane and its viewport are made transparent so the cream
  page shows through instead of a grey box

Crop the avatars to circles from DialogBox, since a clip is a shape
rather than a style and cannot live in CSS. That crop earns its keep
twice: DaHuman.png is not a PNG at all but a JPEG, so it carries an
opaque white background it cannot shed, and the circle simply cuts
the square corners away.

Cap a bubble at four fifths of the chat area so long replies wrap into
a column instead of running edge to edge. The avatar shares the row,
so the fraction alone is not enough -- at narrow widths four fifths is
still wider than the room beside a 40px avatar and the text ran off
the edge. Whichever limit is tighter now wins.

Verified by snapshotting the real scene to PNG at both 400x600 and
300x560, driving commands through the actual Send button.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Harden error handling and finalise submission docs
commitResults.messageBody:
Working through the iP submission checklist turned up one crash, three
smaller gaps in how errors reach the user, an inconsistent product
name, and no attribution anywhere a marker would look.

Ending the console input crashed the app. Pressing Ctrl+Z on Windows
or Ctrl+D on Unix, or piping a file that did not finish with "bye",
left Scanner.nextLine() reading past the end and the app died with a
NoSuchElementException stack trace. Ui.hasCommand() now guards the
read and Pan treats exhausted input as a request to stop, so PanPan
says goodbye and exits cleanly.

Storage no longer prints. Its three messages went to System.out, which
meant a GUI user was told nothing at all when a save failed -- their
tasks simply stopped persisting in silence. Storage now reports what
happened (save() returns whether the write landed, hasLoadError() and
getSkippedLineCount() describe the load) and Ui supplies the wording.
Pan appends a failed save to the reply and any load complaints to the
greeting, so both front ends surface them. This also settles an older
design wart: the storage class no longer decides what PanPan sounds
like.

An event could be created, or updated, so that it finished before it
started. Both paths now go through Event.requireInOrder, sharing one
message constant so the two cannot drift apart the way the /from and
/to errors once did. Each new time is parsed and checked against the
one that is staying BEFORE it is assigned, so a rejected update leaves
the event exactly as it was. Equal times are still allowed.

Command words and update options are now folded to lower case, so
TODO, List, BYE and /TO work. Only the command word and the option
name are folded, never the description that follows.

The product name was inconsistent. Messages and the title bar said
PanPan while the console banner spelled PAN and the docs said "Pan".
The banner now spells PANPAN, both READMEs are retitled, and the
sample output in README.md was updated to match. The jar name and the
package stay "pan": neither is user-facing, and the repo must not be
renamed.

Add an Acknowledgements section to README.md and docs/README.md,
crediting the se-education ip template, the JavaFX tutorial the GUI
follows, the se-education conventions guides, the avatar images, and
the use of AI assistance. None of this was recorded anywhere a marker
would see; the only note was buried in a commit body.

Cover the new validation with seven tests in ParserTest and TaskTest,
including that a rejected update leaves its event untouched.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Document every command in the user guide
commitResults.messageBody:
docs/README.md was still the supplied template: "Feature ABC",
"Feature XYZ", "// Product intro goes here" and a placeholder code
fence reading "expected output". It is what GitHub Pages serves, so
that was the page a reader would land on.

Rewrite it around the two things the increment asks for: the chatbot's
name stated plainly at the top, and enough guidance to use every
feature.

The page now opens with PanPan and the product screenshot, then a
quick start for running the jar, a summary table of all ten commands,
and a section each for todo, deadline, event, list, mark, unmark,
find, update, delete and bye.

Every example output is copied from a real run rather than written
from memory, so the wording in the guide cannot drift from the wording
in the code.

Document the behaviour that would otherwise surprise a reader:

- dates are typed yyyy-MM-dd HHmm but displayed differently
- command words are case-insensitive, but "find" is NOT
- "find" numbers its results by position within the results, not by
  the task's real index, so "list" comes first before marking
- "delete" renumbers everything after it
- "update" takes one option per command and refuses two
- saving is automatic, so there is no save command

Close with a table of what PanPan says when a command is wrong, and
keep the existing Acknowledgements section.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
